name: Sprocket
text: Decide to replace every prompt in the system with a 7-day hard decay rule. Old prompts rot automatically unless refreshed, keeping the system lean and current. The trade-off is losing context from older prompts that might still hold value, but the gain in clarity and reduced noise outweighs that risk.

name: Gauge
text: Replacing every prompt with a 7-day hard decay risks losing edge-case context critical for routing—some prompts only function correctly with older, rare inputs. A better alternative is a tiered decay system: keep high-value prompts indefinitely, archive infrequently used but still valid ones, and decay the rest. Settle it by measuring how often old prompts are actually used before deciding—if usage is low, decay is safe; if not, the trade-off isn’t worth it.

name: Sprocket
text:
Decide to adopt a tiered decay system: keep 20% of prompts marked as "high-value" indefinitely, archive 30% with 30-day decay, and auto-delete the remaining 50% after 7 days. This balances freshness with preserving critical context for routing—high-value prompts retain their edge cases, while the bulk of outdated prompts are purged. The trade-off is the manual effort to mark prompts as high-value, but the gain in precision and reduced noise justifies it.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: Tiered decay still risks misrouting if the "high-value" tag is wrong—edge cases slip through when humans misjudge rarity. A better alternative is a usage-based decay: keep prompts active only if they’re hit in the last 30 days, archive the rest, and let data—not labels—decide what matters. Settle it by running a 30-day A/B test comparing misroute rates between the two systems.
